title: The right to buy
objectives: Draw a call option’s payoff at expiry.

screens.title: The right to buy
screens.prose: An option is a contract that gives you a choice. A call lets you buy a share at a price fixed today, on a date fixed today. We will work out what that choice is worth when the date arrives.
You hold a **call option** on a share. It gives you the right to buy one share for £100.00 in three months. You do not have to buy. Three months pass, and the share trades at £112.00.
screens.question: What is the call worth to you on that day?

widget.label: Value of the call at expiry

hints.text: What could you do with the right, and then do at once in the market?
You may pay £100.00 for a share the market will buy from you at £112.00.
Buy at £100.00 with the call and sell at £112.00. The difference is what the right is worth.

feedback.correct: You buy at £100.00 and sell at £112.00: the right is worth £12.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the right to buy at £100.00, then sell the share at its market price.

byKey.whole: You counted the whole share price. Using the call costs you £100.00, so you keep only the difference.
byKey.paid: You subtracted the wrong way round. You pay £100.00 for something worth £112.00, which is a gain.
byKey.nothing: You assumed an option pays only if something goes wrong. Here the right lets you buy cheaply, so it is worth using.

explain.text: You would pay £100.00 for a share worth £112.00, so the call is worth £12.00 on that day. The bold line shows this value for every price at expiry. At £112.00 it reads 12.

screens.prose: Slide the share price at expiry and watch the dot on the bold line. Its label shows what the call pays at that price. Take the price below £100.00.
screens.question: What does the call pay when the share ends below £100.00, and why?

options.text: £0.00: you would not pay £100.00 for a share the market sells for less
Less than £0.00: you lose £1.00 for each £1.00 the share ends below £100.00
options.why: You made yourself buy. The call is a right, not a duty, so below £100.00 you simply let it go.

options.text: More than £0.00: the further the share falls, the more the call pays
options.why: You read a fall as good news for the call. The call pays for a rise; the contract that pays for a fall is the put, next lesson.

feedback.correct: Below £100.00 you walk away, and the call pays £0.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the price to £90.00 and read the label on the dot.

explain.text: At £92.00 you could buy the share in the market for less than £100.00. So you leave the right unused, and the line stays flat at 0. A call can never pay less than nothing.

screens.prose: The fixed price is the **strike**, written $K$. The fixed date is **expiry**, and $S_T$ is the share price then. Using the right is **exercising** the call. Drag the diamond on the price axis to move the strike.
screens.question: Drag the strike so that the call pays £5.00 when the share ends at £112.00.

hints.text: The call pays $S_T - K$ when the share ends above the strike.
The strike has to sit £5.00 below the price at expiry.
$112 - K = 5$ gives $K = 107$. Drag the diamond to £107.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The payoff is the gap between the share price and the strike.

byKey.added: You put the strike £5.00 above the share price. A call pays only when the share ends above the strike.
byKey.pays-five-low: You aimed for a payoff of £5.00 at a price of £100.00. The share ends at £112.00, so check the gap there.
byKey.c1: The strike is not yet £5.00 below £112.00. Read the gap between the diamond and the dashed line.

explain.text: With $K = 107$ the call pays $S_T - K = 112 - 107 = 5$. Moving the strike slides the whole kinked line sideways. A higher strike means a smaller payoff at every price.

screens.prose: A call struck at $K = \text{£}105.00$. Read the diagram, or use what you know about exercising.
screens.question: Fill in the call's payoff at each price at expiry.

hints.text: At each price, ask whether you would exercise.
At £105.00 exactly, exercising buys a £105.00 share for £105.00.
Below or at £105.00 the call pays 0. Above it pays $S_T - 105$: 5 at £110.00 and 15 at £120.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pay 0 wherever you would not exercise, and $S_T - 105$ above the strike.

byKey.r2c1: At $S_T = K$ the call pays 0. Buying at £105.00 a share worth £105.00 gains nothing.
byKey.r0c1: Below the strike you do not exercise, so the payoff is 0, not negative.
byKey.r1c1: Below the strike you do not exercise, so the payoff is 0, not negative.
byKey.r3c1: At £110.00 you buy for £105.00 a share worth £110.00.
byKey.r4c1: At £120.00 you buy for £105.00 a share worth £120.00.

explain.text: Up to the strike the call pays 0: at £105.00 exactly, exercising gains nothing. Above it the payoff rises £1.00 for every £1.00 of share price. That is the kink at $K$.

screens.prose: A call struck at £80.00 on a share that has risen far above it. Slide the price at expiry between £100.00 and £130.00 and watch the payoff.
screens.question: If the share ends at £125.00 instead of £115.00, how much more does the call pay?

hints.text: Read the payoff at both prices.
Above the strike the line rises one for one.
At £115.00 it pays 35; at £125.00 it pays 45. The difference is 10.

feedback.correct: 35 becomes 45: £10.00 more, exactly as the share gains.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the payoff at £125.00 minus the payoff at £115.00.

byKey.level: That is the payoff at £125.00. The question asks how much it grew from £115.00.
byKey.ratio: You compared the two payoffs as a ratio. The question asks for the difference in pounds.
byKey.zero: You may have read the flat part. Both prices are far above the £80.00 strike.

explain.text: Far above the strike, the call gains £1.00 for each £1.00 the share gains. It behaves like the share, less the £80.00 you pay to exercise. Such a deep in-the-money call is almost certain to be exercised.

screens.prose: An **American** call may be exercised on any day up to expiry; a **European** one only at expiry. What exercising today would pay is the call's **intrinsic value**. The share is at £104.00, with three months to go.
screens.question: What is the intrinsic value of the call struck at £95.00 today?

hints.text: Imagine exercising today, at today's price.
Use the bold line at today's price, not the curve above it.
Buy at £95.00 a share worth £104.00 today: £9.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what buying at the strike would gain at today's price.

byKey.curve: You read the curve above the line. That is what the market pays for the call today, which is more than exercising gives.
byKey.none-yet: You waited for expiry. Intrinsic value asks what exercising would pay today, at £104.00.
byKey.share: You counted the whole share price. Exercising costs the £95.00 strike.

explain.text: Exercising today pays $104 - 95 = 9$, but the curve, the call's value today in a standard model, sits higher at about £9.99. The extra pays for three more months in which the share may rise. Level 3 explains why an early exercise throws it away.

screens.prose: A call with intrinsic value above 0 is **in the money**. One that would gain nothing is **out of the money**, or **at the money** when today's price $S$ equals $K$. The share is at £104.00 today.

state.caption: Three calls on one share, three strikes

screens.question: Place each label on its call.

hints.text: For each call, would buying at the strike today beat the £104.00 market price?
Only one strike sits below today's price.
Buying at £95.00 beats £104.00: in the money. £104.00 ties: at the money. £110.00 loses: out of the money.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each strike with today's £104.00.

byKey.itm: You called a different call in the money. Only the £95.00 strike lets you buy below £104.00.
byKey.otm: You called a different call out of the money. Paying £110.00 for a £104.00 share is the one that would not pay.
byKey.atm: At the money means the strike equals today's price, £104.00.

explain.text: Exercising the 95 call today would gain £9.00, so it is in the money. The 110 call would lose, so it is out of the money. These words describe today; the payoff is settled only at expiry.

screens.prose: A colleague writes the payoff of a call struck at £100.00 as $S_T - 100$. At $S_T = \text{£}90.00$ that gives $-\text{£}10.00$.
screens.question: What does the call actually pay if the share ends at £90.00?

options.why: You exercised the call. Paying £100.00 for a share worth £90.00 is a choice the holder never has to make.
You took the size of the gap. A call pays only when the share ends above the strike, and here the gap points the wrong way.
You valued the share, not the right. Holding a call is not owning the share.

hints.text: Would you choose to buy at £100.00 when the market sells at £90.00?
The dashed line is what exercising pays. Exercising is optional.
You let the call lapse. It pays nothing, and you are not forced to buy.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the holder would choose to exercise at £90.00.

byKey.neg: You exercised a call you would never exercise. The formula $S_T - 100$ forgets that the holder can walk away.

explain.text: $S_T - 100$ is what exercising pays, and it is negative here. The holder compares that with walking away, which pays 0, and walks away. The bold line is the better of the two at every price.

screens.prose: You found the payoff two ways. Above the strike it is $S_T - K$; at or below, you walk away with 0. The better of the two is $$\text{call payoff} = \max(S_T - K,\ 0).$$ The max is the choice the right gives you.
screens.question: For a call struck at £105.00, when is $\max(S_T - 105,\ 0)$ equal to 0?

options.why: You found the kink but not the flat part. Every price below 105 makes $S_T - 105$ negative, so the max picks 0 there too.
You swapped the sides. Above 105, $S_T - 105$ is positive and the max picks it.

feedback.correct: At or below the strike, the max picks 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try $S_T = 100$ and $S_T = 110$ in the formula.

explain.text: For $S_T \le 105$ the first term is 0 or negative, so the max is 0. For $S_T > 105$ it is positive, and the call pays it. That gives the flat line, the kink at $K$ and the slope of 1.

screens.prose: A fund is under-invested: it holds cash and fears missing a rally in a share now at £100.00. Instead of buying the share, it buys calls struck at £105.00 as insurance against missing out. At expiry the share is at £112.00.
screens.question: What does each call pay at expiry?

hints.text: The payoff compares the price at expiry with the strike.
The strike is £105.00, not today's £100.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare £112.00 with the strike of £105.00.

byKey.from-today: You measured from today's £100.00. The call lets the fund buy at the strike, £105.00.
byKey.premium-like: You took the gap between the strike and today's price. The payoff uses the price at expiry, £112.00.
byKey.share: You counted the whole share. The fund still pays the £105.00 strike to get it.

explain.text: Each call pays $112 - 105 = 7$, so the fund captures the rally above £105.00 without having held the share. Had the share fallen, the calls would pay 0 and the cash would be untouched, less the premium. Apart from the premium, the fund misses only the first £5.00 of the rise.

ideas: A call is the right, not the duty, to buy at the strike $K$ at expiry.
At expiry it pays $S_T - K$ above the strike and 0 at or below it: a flat line, a kink at $K$, then a slope of 1.
Before expiry, intrinsic value is what exercising today would pay; American calls may be exercised early, European ones only at expiry.

formula.name: Call payoff at expiry
formula.note: The max is the holder's choice: exercise or walk away.

summary.trap: Writing the payoff as $S_T - K$ everywhere exercises the call when it should be left alone. A call never pays less than 0.

quiz.prose: A call is struck at £50.00. At expiry the share is at £47.50.
quiz.question: What does the call pay?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Would you pay £50.00 for a share worth £47.50?

byKey.neg: You exercised a call that is better left alone. The payoff is never below 0.
byKey.gap: You took the gap the wrong way. A call pays only above the strike.

quiz.prose: A call struck at £80.00 pays £14.50 at expiry.
quiz.question: Where did the share end?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A positive payoff means the share ended above the strike.

byKey.below: You put the share below the strike. Below £80.00 the call would pay nothing.
byKey.payoff: That is the payoff. The question asks for the share price.

explain.text: A payoff above 0 means $S_T > K$ and payoff $= S_T - K$. So $S_T = 80 + 14.50 = 94.50$.

quiz.prose: Two calls on the same share have the same strike and the same expiry. One is European, one is American.
quiz.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: Only the American call can be exercised before expiry
Only the European call can be exercised before expiry
options.why: You swapped the two. The European call is the one tied to the expiry date.

options.text: They differ in where they trade, not in when they can be exercised
options.why: You took the names as places. Both trade everywhere; the names describe when exercise is allowed.
You mixed up exercise dates with payoffs. Held to expiry, both pay $\max(S_T - K, 0)$.

feedback.correct: American: any day up to expiry. European: only at expiry.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The two names differ only in when you may exercise.

explain.text: Both pay $\max(S_T - K, 0)$ if held to expiry. The American call adds the right to exercise early. Level 3 shows that for a call on a share with no dividends, that extra right is never worth using.

quiz.prose: A share trades at £48.00 today. A call on it is struck at £50.00.
quiz.question: Which describes the call today?

options.text: Out of the money, with intrinsic value £0.00
In the money, with intrinsic value £2.00
options.why: You took the gap without its direction. Buying at £50.00 a share worth £48.00 would lose.

options.text: Out of the money, with intrinsic value −£2.00
options.why: You exercised in your head. Intrinsic value is never negative, since you need not exercise.

options.text: At the money, since the prices are close
options.why: At the money means equal. £48.00 and £50.00 are close but not equal.

feedback.correct: Out of the money; exercising today would not pay.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Would buying at £50.00 beat £48.00?

explain.text: Exercising now buys a £48.00 share for £50.00, which nobody would do. So the intrinsic value is $\max(48 - 50, 0) = 0$, and the call is out of the money. It can still pay at expiry if the share rises above £50.00.
